title: Exceptions
cards/0/body: If a task fails, await throws its exception: the very one thrown inside. A plain try/catch around the await catches it.
cards/1/body:
If you wait synchronously with .Result or .Wait(), the exception arrives wrapped in an AggregateException, with the original inside, in InnerExceptions.

GetAwaiter().GetResult() throws the original exception, but it still blocks the thread.
cards/2/q: Will this catch block catch a network error?
cards/2/options/0: No: .Result throws AggregateException, with the HttpRequestException inside
cards/2/explain: One more reason not to block: deadlocks and awkward exceptions.
cards/3/task: Start three requests with Task.WhenAll and make two of them fail. How many exceptions does await throw, and how many are stored in the task?
cards/4/q: WhenAll, and A and C failed. What does await throw?
cards/4/options/0: Only A's exception; all errors are in the WhenAll task's Exception.InnerExceptions
cards/4/explain: await unwraps and throws the first one. To see them all, keep the WhenAll task and check its Exception.
cards/5/body:
If nobody awaits a task, nobody sees its exception. Since .NET 4.5 this doesn't crash the app; the error is simply lost (you can catch it with the TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException event).

That's why fire-and-forget hides errors.
cards/6/q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
cards/6/options/2: A WhenAll task keeps all errors in Exception.InnerExceptions
cards/6/options/3: An exception from an unawaited task crashes the app at once
cards/6/explain: With await, try/catch works just as it does in synchronous code.
cards/7/pairs/2/1: The original, but the thread is blocked
cards/7/pairs/3/1: An error from a task nobody awaited
